title: How Much Will You Actually Change in Ten Years?
metaTitle: How Much Will You Change in Ten Years? The Research
metaDescription: Probably more than you expect. The 'end of history illusion' shows people underestimate how much their values, tastes, and personality will keep changing.
keyFinding: At every age people acknowledge they have changed a lot in the past decade but predict they will change little in the next — and the research shows they are usually wrong, underestimating future change in values, tastes, and personality.
honestAnswer: Probably more than you expect. People are reasonably good at seeing how much they have changed over the past decade, but they consistently underestimate how much they will keep changing over the next one. Your values, preferences, and even aspects of your personality are likely to keep shifting — gradually, but more than your current self predicts.

This holds at every age. Whether you are 20 or 60, you tend to feel like you have basically arrived at the 'real' you, while in fact change continues. The honest implication is to hold your current preferences and plans a little more loosely, because the person they are for is still moving.
whatDataShows: The clearest evidence comes from Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson's 2013 study, which named this the 'end of history illusion.' Across a large sample spanning a wide age range, people reported having changed substantially over the previous ten years but predicted they would change relatively little over the next ten — in their personality, values, and preferences alike. Comparing predictions with what people of an age decade older actually reported showed the predictions systematically too small. People treat the present as the endpoint of their development when it is just a waypoint.

Personality research supports the underlying point that change keeps happening. Brent Roberts's work describes a 'maturity principle': across adulthood, people tend on average to become somewhat more conscientious, emotionally stable, and agreeable. The shifts are gradual and not dramatic year to year, but they accumulate, and they continue well into later life rather than locking in early.

So both halves fit together. Personality and preferences genuinely do keep changing across the lifespan, and at the same time people reliably predict that their own change is about to stop. The result is a recurring mismatch between how much you expect to change and how much you actually will.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It feels like you have finished changing because remembering is easier than imagining. You can look back and see concretely how your tastes, opinions, and relationships shifted, but you cannot vividly picture changes you have not lived yet — so the future self defaults to looking a lot like the present one. The asymmetry between recalled change and imagined change is exactly what produces the illusion.

There is also a comfort to feeling settled. Believing you have arrived at your true self makes the present feel stable and your current choices feel safe; admitting you will keep changing introduces uncertainty about whether today's preferences will still fit. The illusion is partly motivated — it is reassuring to feel done.

And because the change is gradual, it is hard to feel it happening in real time. Personality and values drift slowly enough that day to day you feel constant, even though across a decade the cumulative shift is substantial. You only notice the distance after it has opened up.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The practical takeaway from this research is to make decisions that leave room for a future self who may want different things. Reversible choices, and plans that do not lock in a single identity or preference forever, tend to age better precisely because the person they are for will keep moving. Holding current tastes and ambitions a little loosely is the rational response to the evidence.

It is also worth being cautious about permanent commitments justified by 'I'll always feel this way.' The end-of-history finding suggests that intuition is unreliable in a predictable direction — you will probably feel differently than you expect about at least some of it. Building in the option to revisit big choices respects how much you are likely to change.

On the encouraging side, the same research is a reason for optimism if you are unhappy with where you are now. Continued change is the default, not the exception, and the maturity principle suggests the average drift is toward greater stability and conscientiousness. The current version of you is not the final one.
whatDoesNotHelp: Assuming your present preferences are permanent does not help, because the evidence says they probably are not. Anchoring big, hard-to-reverse decisions to 'this is who I am and always will be' systematically overweights a self that the research shows will keep changing.

Expecting dramatic, sudden reinvention is the opposite error and is no more accurate. The maturity principle describes gradual, cumulative change, not overnight transformation. Waiting for a sudden shift in who you are, or assuming change requires a wake-up moment, misreads how the process actually works.

Treating the end-of-history illusion as a reason to make no plans at all does not follow either. The point is not that the future is unknowable, but that your future preferences are more movable than they feel — which argues for flexible, revisable plans, not for no plans.
realNumbersInContext: There is no single statistic that captures this; the finding is about a direction of error. In Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson's 2013 study, at essentially every age people predicted they would change less over the coming decade than people just a decade older reported actually having changed. The gap between predicted and actual change is the headline result — and it pointed the same way at every age.

Roberts's maturity-principle research adds the underlying trend: across adulthood, average personality drifts gradually toward more conscientiousness, emotional stability, and agreeableness. The shifts are modest in any given year but accumulate over a decade. Both lines of evidence say the same thing — you will likely change more in the next ten years than your current self predicts, so plans and preferences are worth holding loosely.

faqs.question: Will I really change much in the next ten years?
faqs.answer: The research suggests you will likely change more than you currently predict. The 'end of history illusion' (Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson, 2013) found that at every age people acknowledge a lot of past change but expect little future change in their values, tastes, and personality — and that prediction is usually too small.

faqs.question: What is the end of history illusion?
faqs.answer: It is the tendency to feel you have basically finished developing — to recognise how much you have changed over the past decade while predicting you will change little in the next. It appears at essentially every age, which means most people are treating the present self as a final version when it is still in motion.

faqs.question: Does personality actually keep changing in adulthood?
faqs.answer: Yes, gradually. Brent Roberts's research describes a 'maturity principle': across adulthood people tend on average to become somewhat more conscientious, emotionally stable, and agreeable. The changes are slow and cumulative rather than dramatic, and they continue well into later life rather than locking in early.

faqs.question: If I'll change anyway, why make any plans?
faqs.answer: The finding argues for flexible plans, not no plans. Because your future preferences are more movable than they feel, decisions that stay reversible and don't lock in a single identity tend to age better. The point is to leave room for a future self who may want different things, not to stop deciding.

faqs.question: Is it good news or bad news that I'll keep changing?
faqs.answer: It can be reassuring. If you are unhappy with where you are now, continued change is the default rather than the exception, and the average drift is toward greater stability and conscientiousness. It does mean current preferences should be held loosely — but it also means the present version of you is not the final one.

dataSources: Quoidbach, J., Gilbert, D. T., & Wilson, T. D. (2013). The End of History Illusion. Science, 339(6115), 96–98.
Roberts, B. W. — research on personality change across the lifespan and the maturity principle (gradual increases in conscientiousness, emotional stability, and agreeableness in adulthood).
